title: SPECIAL REPORT: Inside AI scam ads exploiting TikTok’s advertising system to defraud Nigerians

reading.body:
This is an impersonation failure at the advertising layer of a social platform. The ads used deepfake video and cloned voices to present themselves as banks, telecoms brands and public figures, and they were distributed as paid promotions rather than as organic posts. The harm occurred after the click, when victims handed over account details or contact information in response to offers of grants, loans, giveaways and investment returns.

The failure sits in advertiser verification and in content moderation for local languages. The ads ran in English, Pidgin, Yoruba and Hausa, and the reporting notes gaps in moderating local-language content alongside weak verification of who is placing an ad. Many ads carried no AI label and had comments disabled, which removed two of the cheaper signals a reviewer or a user could have used. Catching this would have required checking advertiser identity before the ads ran, and reviewing paid promotions in each language they were bought in rather than only in the platform's best-supported ones.

What is not established is the platform's knowledge of any individual ad, or the identity and intent of the advertisers, none of whom are named as having been identified or charged. The loss figures come from two victims who spoke to the reporter, and the count of archived ads is the reporter's own sample over five weeks, not a platform total.

reports.title: SPECIAL REPORT: Inside AI scam ads exploiting TikTok’s advertising system to defraud Nigerians

summary:
A Premium Times investigation found that AI-generated scam ads are running as paid promotions on TikTok and defrauding Nigerians. Fraudsters impersonate brands such as OPay, UBA, MTN and Airtel, plus public figures like Aliko Dangote and the Emir of Kano, using deepfake videos and cloned voices. One victim, Mohammed Yusuf, lost about N150,000 after submitting his OPay details to a fake grant ad. Another, Ahmad Wura, lost roughly N1 million in cryptocurrency after entering his email through a similar ad. The reporter archived 130 such ads over five weeks, with OPay appearing in 28 of them.

The ads promised grants, loans, giveaways and investment returns, and appeared in English, Pidgin, Yoruba and Hausa. Many had comments disabled, no AI labels, and untraceable advertiser details. Nigeria loses over $500 million yearly to scams, according to NITDA. Experts blamed weak advertiser verification, gaps in moderating local-language content, and rapid AI advances. The article does not say what happens next, though experts called for stronger laws and platform accountability.
